Mike--

I always love the puns in the Comments section, but you also definitely GO BIG as a constructor!

For me, it was a classic fast-slow-fast solve.  The 11-letter stacked entries at the top and bottom just leapt into the puzzle for me, while the middle befuddled me for quite a while.

Please keep the puzzles coming (and no slacking off on the pun comments just because you're a big shot constructor now).
Congratulations, Mike! You regularly make the comment section a better place and your puzzle helped my day end on a fun note. Thank you!

I found that to be a worthy challenge of a Friday puzzle especially coming back from a party before tackling the puzzle. I thought many of the clue/answer combos were positively inspired, and it often took me a few mental iterations before I could see through the deception. Looking forward to more from this constructor!
Tricky at first but flowed nicely once I broke in. CANT TOP THAT!
A little slower than my Friday average but thoroughly enjoyable!
Fun time. Not tough and not a breeze. Thanks.

Congrats, Mike, on your debut. The NW and SE stacks of the expressions are an architectural marvel, with CEREAL AISLE being the only misfit. But like Sean, this was my favorite clue, although I'm surprised to hear your favorite is Cinnamon Toast Crunch. I thought "Mikey" would like Life.

CHEERIO Mike! Congrats on your debut!

I’ve been touting Mike’s Crosshare puzzles lately and telling him I’m surprised he never published and he never let on he had one in the works! While his own puzzles have more of his devilish puns, this one certainly showed his humor, “WHIT” (or should I say it was very WHEATY) and had plenty of TRIX. 

It’s a measure of how much I am on the same wavelength (perhaps a dubious admission) that when I saw “Total area” I immediately jumped to something with cereal. But then I thought, no question mark, fairly brand-y…NAH, can’t be. I’m so glad they kept it!

Lots of other CRUNCHy clues that I wouldn’t be surprised came straight from Mike—formal guidance, stacked deck, relief pitcher—that certainly CHEX out with his sense of humor. Fun grid too. Not terribly hard, but certainly not a PUFF piece.

Hope this is your LUCKY CHARM Mike and we see plenty more from you, I can see it’s a LIFElong passion. To misquote the commercial—“Hey Mikey, I like it!”

(Will this unRAISINably long POST ever end? Nah, it’s a CEREAL!)

14:31 for a Friday is not just a great time for me, it's a testament to the telegraphic (and fun) clues, the smooth fill, and to my mind, zero glue.

Special shoutout to both triple-stacks!

Grazie, Graczyk!

Is it just me, or are the “quotation” clues getting out of hand lately? There are 10 today (11 if you count the dog guarding its kibble). I don’t mind them mixed in once in a while, but I don’t find them fun in large quantities - especially when they dominate the long answers.

Congratulations on your debut Mike! I didn’t think I’d get anywhere with all those long answers, but a few clues in and I was getting them and really enjoyed the struggle and the  of the puns. Total area… I’m gonna be laughing about that for a while.

Mike?!! THE Mike?!

So glad I loved this puzzle because you’re a true legend of Wordplay.

I didn’t recognize the name but, lo and behold, it turns out to be a very familiar part of our little family 👍

Well done, Mike!

Congrats to the Munster punster! A delightful first foray. Hoping it's not your last. Also hoping you don't slack on your responsibilities to the Wordplay column just because you're, you know, a real celeb now.

That’s a lot of fun packed into a Friday, Munster Mike.  

Great debut.

Then I remembered that Tostitos with salsa and CHEESEDIP is my go to dinner/late night snack during the Australian Open. Mike from Munster wrote some puns
That rivaled damn near anyone’s.
But then that punster made a puzz
And set the Wordplay world abuzz.
“So great,” they cried. “We all done did it!
Please make another and submit it.
And with a bit of skill and luck, sir
You’ll be a cereal constructor.”

Well, that was well nigh impenetrable at first attempt. Thank goodness my Lit nerd credentials knew ANAPHORA. Being European gave me the French ins and I managed a few crosses from those, but there was far too much white space for my liking.
The last and worst entries were of course the US specific food stuffs, as complete unknowns. They’re completely appropriate for a US publication, but the seventh circle of hell for the rest of us.
Bouillabaisse is a STEW? Ok. As far as I’m concerned it’s a soup; vile, smelly and my husband’s favourite, so frequently stinks up the house. Yuk.

All the above notwithstanding, well done Mike on an outstanding debut. A cracking Friday offering.

This one gave me fits.  I was nearly done in by the brand name references, but once I got ROLAIDS and CEREALAISLE I had to chuckle at the clues.  You might say that the Total clue, like the rest of the puzzle was chewy.  I also loved the clues for DRESSCODE and SAILORS.  The NE was sticky because in addition to stumbling on ROLAIDS I couldn’t remember ANAPHORA from my English major days and I tried iota instead of WHIT.

Anyway congrats to Punster Mike who brings us so much joy on a daily basis.

Mike: congrats on the debut! I’ll echo others in saying that TOTAL was a phenomenal entry, and the quality of this grid was very high in general.

On the off chance you see this and are willing to share, I’d be tremendously interested to hear a bit about the editorial process this puzzle went through. In particular, does the final product reflect the level of challenge you were aiming for, or did the editors significantly dial down the clueing difficulty? I’m especially curious about that since this is a themeless (i.e. it seems fair to assume you were targeting a Friday or Saturday publication date).

Oh, and very middle-of-the-night I got back to yesterday's "inclined plane" business.  Clearly, I was working on a very elementary level, which was pointed out only in the kindest of ways.  The challenge of teaching "slow learners" often means that special ed students get very little beyond basic subjects.  I believe that you can teach just about anything if you can break it down well enough..so we had science units....  but after I retired, when I paid a drop-in visit to my last class (multi-handicapped middle graders at Children's Rehad Hospital), the teacher had them painting in coloring books... sigh.

Mike from Munster! As if we didn’t love you enough, you had to throw in a fabulous Friday puzzle. For me, this was one of those days when the puzzle, the column, and the constructor notes are all winners. Thanks, Mike and Sean!

A gorgeous, beautifully meshed grid, tricky clues, and no crosswordese.  What's not to love?

The cleverest clues and answers weren't necessarily the ones that gave me the most trouble.  I especially loved CEREAL AISLE (which I didn't see for along time); DRESS CODE (which I did see); SAILORS; and the easy but lovely I MET SOMEONE.

The answer that got written over the most was "scintilla", which started out as IOTA, then became HINT (based on OH COME ON plus the final T), which then belatedly became WHIT.  ANAPHORA is what that rhetorical device is called?  Who knew?

Today I learned NADA COLADA, which I think is absolutely adorable.  Have you ever noticed that the alcohol-free cocktails have the best names?  But names aside, I do want the PINA in my Colada and the BLOODY in my Mary.

A beautifully made puzzle -- a great themeless in every way.  Was sorry when it was over.

One more puzzle find - perhaps the most amazing I've ever encountered. A Sunday from July 4(!), 2004 by Elizabeth C. Gorski. First - there were 4 connected down 'reveal' answers, each of those 11 letters and placed synchronously on opposite sides of the puzzle. The clue for those answers: 3-down -"With 86-, 17- and 91-down, how to 'illustrate' this puzzle". And then those 4 answers, each of them 11 letters - DRAWSTARSON THETHIRTEEN ABBREVIATED COLONYNAMES And those 'colony names' were each two-letter abbreviations, placed in a synchronous circle around the middle of the puzzle. And there were some other theme-related answers. Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=7/4/2004&h=86d .....
